subject: Climate & Environment
title: Can We Reverse Deforestation
description: A quick, practical guide to Can We Reverse Deforestation.

hook.text: Costa Rica was losing its forests fast in the 1980s. Then it tried something radical.

buildup.text: The government paid landowners to keep their trees standing — cash for conservation.

discovery.text: Forest cover doubled from 26% to over 52% in just three decades.

twist.text: The recovered forests now power a booming ecotourism industry worth billions.

climax.text: What Costa Rica proved is that deforestation is a choice — and choices can be reversed.

punchline.text: One country proved that forests can come back. The rest just need to choose.

quiz.question: How did Costa Rica double its forest cover?
options: Paying landowners to keep trees standing

details.summary: Reversing global deforestation is technically and economically feasible but requires transforming food systems, ending illegal clearing, financing protection in developing nations, and making standing forests worth more than the land beneath them.
details.whyItMatters: Deforestation can be stopped. The question is whether political and economic systems will prioritize forests before critical tipping points are crossed.
takeaways: Brazil cut Amazon deforestation 80 percent between 2004 and 2012
Yield improvements could free farmland for forest recovery
Standing forest must become more economically valuable than clearing

faq.question: Has any country successfully reversed deforestation?
faq.answer: Several countries have increased net forest cover, including China, India, and Costa Rica. Brazil achieved an 80 percent reduction in Amazon deforestation between 2004 and 2012 through enforcement, monitoring, and supply chain pressure before backsliding.

faq.question: How much would it cost to end tropical deforestation?
faq.answer: Estimates range from 30 to 50 billion dollars per year in direct conservation spending, payments to communities, and enforcement costs. This is a fraction of the trillions in ecosystem services that intact tropical forests provide annually.
